vendas-marketing-operacoes-conflito.title: Why sales, marketing, and operations are always in conflict (and how to fix it)
vendas-marketing-operacoes-conflito.excerpt: Marketing generates leads, sales complains about quality. Sales closes the deal, operations can't deliver. See the causes and how to fix it.
vendas-marketing-operacoes-conflito.content:
Sales, marketing, and operations live in conflict when their individual metrics contradict each other, when information crosses from area to area manually, and when no one owns shared indicators. Marketing generates leads, sales complains about quality. Sales closes a deal with an aggressive deadline, operations cannot deliver. Operations demands a fix, sales blames marketing for bringing in a bad client. The conflict is not between people, it is between incentives.

This article is for business owners who recognize the recurring cycle of "each area blaming the other" and want to understand the structural cause, not the surface. Next: the classic tension tripod among the three areas, the 4 causes that sustain the conflict, and the framework to align them.

The classic tension tripod

In a mid-size B2B company, three tensions show up repeatedly:

Tension 1, Marketing vs Sales

Marketing complains: "we generate plenty of leads, sales doesn't convert". Sales complains: "the leads aren't qualified, we waste time with people who aren't going to buy". The monthly meeting becomes a forum for accusations.

Structural cause: marketing is measured by lead volume, sales by conversion rate. Contradictory incentives. Marketing maximizes volume (which can include bad leads). Sales filters bad leads (which reduces accepted volume).

Resolution: a shared metric, "qualified lead that became an opportunity". Both areas win when that number goes up.

Tension 2, Sales vs Operations

Sales complains: "operations can't deliver on the deadline I promised". Operations complains: "sales promises impossible things without checking capacity".

Structural cause: sales is measured by closed volume, operations by SLA met. When sales closes an aggressive deal, operations inherits an impossible problem. When operations refuses, sales blames them for "getting in the way of the deal".

Resolution: sales only promises within capacity that operations confirmed in real time. An integrated platform shows capacity to the salesperson at the moment of the proposal.

Tension 3, Operations vs Customer Service

Operations delivers on the technical deadline. Customer service gets a client complaining that what was delivered doesn't meet expectations. Operations says "we delivered what was requested". Customer service says "the client wanted something else".

Structural cause: the specification of what the client wanted lives in a system separate from what operations executes. Translation between the two is manual and loses information.

Resolution: the client's specification, the production order, and the promised SLA live in the same system. Operations sees what the client expects, not only what was technically requested.

The 4 structural causes of conflict

1. Metrics with contradictory incentives. Each area optimizes locally, the global sum degrades. Conflict is a mathematical result of the incentives.

2. Separate systems that don't share context. Sales in the CRM, operations in the ERP, marketing in an automation tool, customer service in a helpdesk. Information crosses manually. Context is lost along the way.

3. Lack of standardized cross-functional processes. When a lead becomes an opportunity, what happens? When a sale closes, what gets triggered? Without a formal process, each area improvises, and one area's improvisation hurts another.

4. Absence of a regular cross-functional ritual. Without cadence, areas only talk when a problem appears. Preventive conversation doesn't exist. Reactive is too late.

The framework to align (4 concrete actions)

Action 1, Create 3-5 shared metrics across areas. Each area keeps its individual metrics + shared metrics that go into everyone's bonus. Example: marketing + sales share "qualified lead converted into opportunity". Sales + operations share "% of delivery on the promised deadline". Operations + customer service share "NPS by product line".

Action 2, Standardize 5 critical cross-functional processes. Lead → sales, sales → operations, operations → finance, customer service → sales (account), finance → sales (commission). Each with an owner, trigger, deliverable, SLA.

Action 3, Establish a weekly cross-functional meeting. 30-45 minutes, leaders of the critical areas, focused on preventive coordination. Agenda: what will happen this week that affects other areas, what I need from other areas, cross-functional decisions that need to be made.

Action 4, Migrate to an integrated platform if you are still on separate systems. Areas that see the same information in real time conflict less than areas that depend on manual communication.

How agentic AI changes this dynamic

Three specific capabilities:

1. Proactive cross-functional notification. When an event in one area affects another, the agent warns before it becomes a problem. "Salesperson A just closed 3 contracts with an aggressive SLA. Operations: capacity is 75% committed for this week. I recommend talking before this becomes a problem."

2. Context translation between areas. "When sales asks for 'urgency' it usually means a sensitive relationship. Operations: treat this as an emotional priority, not only a technical one."

3. Detection of recurring conflict patterns. If sales vs operations has a recurring conflict about the same client, the agent identifies it and proposes a structural adjustment.

Next steps

  1. Identify which of the 3 classic tensions is strongest in your company. Focus on the main one first.
  2. Define 3-5 shared metrics between the areas in conflict.
  3. Establish a weekly cross-functional meeting if you don't have one yet.

The worst decision is to keep treating as a "cultural problem" what is a structural problem.

Want to see areas talking in real time on a single platform?

A 30-minute demo. Orbit + Olívia shows how sales, marketing, operations, and customer service operate with the same information. Companies with R$500k+/month leave with an applicable diagnosis.

Schedule a demo →

Frequently asked questions

Why do marketing and sales live in conflict?

Contradictory incentives. Marketing is measured by lead volume, sales by conversion rate. Solution: a shared metric "qualified lead converted into opportunity".

Why do sales and operations clash?

Sales is measured by closing, operations by SLA. Sales closes aggressively, operations inherits the impossible. Solution: sales only promises within the capacity that operations confirmed in real time.

How do you align areas that live in conflict?

Four actions: 3-5 shared metrics in the bonus, 5 standardized cross-functional processes, a weekly cross-functional meeting, an integrated platform where everyone sees the same information.

Is the conflict cultural or structural?

Structural, in the vast majority of cases. People in well-designed systems collaborate. People in poorly designed systems conflict, regardless of individual good intentions.

Do shared metrics work?

Yes. When 20-30% of the bonus depends on a metric shared with another area, areas naturally align. When 100% is individual, areas optimize locally and the global sum degrades.

Can AI mediate conflict between areas?

In part. An agent identifies recurring conflict patterns, translates context between areas, and anticipates a cross-functional problem. It doesn't replace human conversation, but it drastically reduces situations where conflict only becomes a problem after it has already exploded.

How long does it take to align?

Shared metrics and a weekly ritual: effect in 60-90 days. Integrated platform: 3-6 months. Changing incentives (bonus) is what most quickly changes behavior, before technology.

What to do when one area refuses to align?

Usually a signal of a specific leadership problem, not a structural one. If metrics are aligned and the ritual exists but resistance persists, it is time for a performance conversation with the leader of the area that is resisting.

software-bpms-como-escolher.title: BPMS software: how to choose a process management platform in 2026
software-bpms-como-escolher.excerpt: Standalone BPMS, an ERP module, or an integrated platform? See a practical comparison and how to choose process management software.
software-bpms-como-escolher.content:
To choose BPMS (Business Process Management System) software, differentiate three categories: traditional standalone BPMS (Bizagi, Camunda, Bonitasoft), a good fit for companies with complex processes and dedicated IT; a BPMS module inside an ERP (TOTVS Fluig, SAP Workflow), a good fit for ERP-centric companies; and BPMS in a modern integrated management platform (Orbit and similar), a good fit for B2B companies that want processes natively connected to CRM, finance, and KPIs. The wrong choice becomes yet another process silo disconnected from the rest of the operation.

This article is for managers choosing a BPMS for the first time or replacing the current one. Next: the 3 categories with strengths and weaknesses, a practical comparison, decision criteria, and how agentic AI changes the game.

The 3 BPMS categories

Category 1, Traditional standalone BPMS (Bizagi, Camunda, Bonitasoft, IBM BPM)

Systems dedicated to process management. Robust capabilities in BPMN modeling, execution, monitoring, and optimization. They often require dedicated IT to implement and maintain.

When it makes sense: a company with very complex processes (banking, insurance, heavy industry), dedicated IT with customization capacity, a need for advanced modeling.

Strengths: technical depth, advanced customization, capacity for complex processes.

Weaknesses: requires a technical team, isolated from other areas, UX frequently dated.

Cost: R$5-50k/month depending on scale, + implementation and analyst cost (R$10-30k/month).

Category 2, BPMS module in an ERP (TOTVS Fluig, SAP Workflow)

Process capability inside a larger ERP. It leverages data and users already in the ERP.

When it makes sense: a company that already has a strong central ERP and processes revolve around the ERP.

Strengths: native integration with finance/accounting, market standard in industry.

Weaknesses: dated UX, limited customization, processes outside the ERP's scope stay outside.

Cost: generally included in the ERP license, but the ERP itself is expensive.

Category 3, BPMS in a modern integrated management platform (Orbit and similar)

BPMS as a native module of a single platform that combines processes + CRM + finance + KPIs + HR + agentic AI.

When it makes sense: a Brazilian B2B company of R$500k+/month with 30-300 employees, looking to reduce the total number of tools, valuing native integration, wanting embedded agentic AI.

Strengths: process connected to real data (CRM, finance), execution inside the same system, agentic AI monitors and suggests optimization, competitive total cost.

Weaknesses: less depth in highly specific capabilities vs standalone BPMS.

Cost: R$3-15k/month for the whole company (not per user).

Practical comparison

Criterion Standalone BPMS BPMS in ERP BPMS in an integrated platform
Advanced BPMN modeling Strong Medium Strong
CRM integration Via API Manual Native
Finance integration Via API Native Native
KPI integration Via API Limited Native
Agentic AI Some Rare Yes
Requires dedicated IT Yes Medium No
Cost (40 employees) R$15-80k/month Included in ERP (expensive) R$3-15k/month total
Suitable for Large industrial company ERP-centric company B2B 30-300+ employees

How to choose: 5 criteria

1. Process complexity. Highly customized processes with complex logic: standalone BPMS. Typical administrative processes: BPMS in an integrated platform covers them well.

2. Internal technical maturity. Dedicated IT team: any path. No IT: an integrated platform is the only viable option.

3. Importance of integration with other areas. Isolated processes: standalone BPMS works. Processes that need to talk to CRM/finance/KPIs in real time: an integrated platform.

4. Total cost over 3 years. Add license + implementation + analyst + maintenance. In a mid-size B2B company, an integrated platform frequently wins.

5. Implementation speed. Standalone: 6-12 months. ERP: included in the ERP rollout. Integrated platform: 1-3 months.

How agentic AI changes BPMS in 2026

Three new capabilities:

1. Mapping through conversational interview. An agent interviews the team and builds the flow automatically. What used to take days with standalone BPMS takes hours.

2. Continuous bottleneck detection. "Process X is averaging 4.3 days in stage Y, with 80% of the delay in legal review. Suggestion: create an automatic path for cases below R$X."

3. Pattern-based optimization suggestions. The agent compares with similar companies (anonymized) and suggests adjustments.

Next steps

  1. Identify process complexity. Highly customized? Typical of a B2B company?
  2. Assess internal IT. Do you have a dedicated team or not?
  3. Calculate total cost over 3 years. Include everything.
  4. Book a demo of the 2 main options. Decide by watching the tool in operation, not on a slide.

The worst decision is buying an expensive standalone BPMS when the company only needs the typical processes of a Brazilian B2B business.

Want to see native BPMS in an integrated platform with AI?

A 30-minute demo. Orbit + Olívia show BPMS connected to CRM, finance, and KPIs in a single platform. Companies of R$500k+/month leave with an applicable diagnosis.

Schedule a demo →

Frequently asked questions

What is BPMS?

Business Process Management System: software to model, execute, monitor, and optimize business processes. It combines design (BPMN), automation, monitoring, and analytics capabilities in one platform.

What are the best BPMS on the market?

It depends on the profile. Traditional standalone: Bizagi, Camunda, Bonitasoft. In ERP: TOTVS Fluig, SAP Workflow. Modern integrated platform: Orbit and similar. For a Brazilian B2B of R$500k+/month, an integrated platform usually wins on cost-benefit.

How much does BPMS cost?

Traditional standalone: R$15-80k/month (license + analyst). ERP: included, but the ERP itself costs R$3-30k/month. Integrated platform: R$3-15k/month for the whole company (includes other areas).

Does BPMS replace ERP?

No. BPMS manages processes. ERP manages financial/tax transactions. The two are complementary. A modern integrated platform combines BPMS + ERP-like capabilities in a unified architecture for B2B services.

How long does it take to implement BPMS?

Standalone: 6-12 months. In ERP: included in the rollout. Integrated platform: 1-3 months. Time depends more on process maturity than on the technology.

Does BPMS need dedicated IT?

Traditional standalone: yes, it requires an analyst. ERP: depends on the ERP. Modern integrated platform: designed to operate without dedicated IT. For B2B of 30-100 employees without IT, an integrated platform is the only realistic option.

How does AI change BPMS in 2026?

Three capabilities: mapping through conversational interview (from days to hours), continuous bottleneck detection, pattern-based optimization suggestions.

When should you switch BPMS?

When the current tool clearly falls short: slowness, no mobile, no integration with other areas, high maintenance cost, low adoption. 3+ of these signs present suggest a migration.

plataformas-comunicacao-corporativa.title: Platforms to align departments: how to choose corporate communication in 2026
plataformas-comunicacao-corporativa.excerpt: Slack, Microsoft Teams, or an AI-integrated platform? See when each one makes sense and how to choose the right tool to align teams.
plataformas-comunicacao-corporativa.content:
To choose a corporate communication platform that actually aligns departments, you need to distinguish three categories: corporate chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams), good for everyday human communication but it does not solve information fragmentation; process platforms (Notion, Asana, ClickUp), good for documentation and tasks but they do not solve operational data; and an integrated management platform with embedded chat (Orbit and similar), good for aligning areas because it connects communication to real operational data. The wrong choice becomes extra noise. The right choice eliminates “nobody told me” situations.

This article is for managers who already understand that cross-department communication needs a tool, but are confused among the options on the market. Below: the 3 different categories (often confused), how to choose, and what changes with agentic AI.

The 3 categories of corporate communication platform

Category 1, Corporate chat (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord)

Real-time messaging platforms. Good for: quick conversation, one-off questions, status updates, everyday human communication. They replace informal email and corporate WhatsApp.

Strengths: modern UX, calendar integration, history search, online presence, threads.

Weaknesses: they do not solve operational data (a salesperson asks in Slack but the data lives in a separate CRM), information gets lost in the scroll, creation of “channel islands” that become new silos.

Typical cost: R$30–100 per user/month.

Category 2, Process and task platforms (Notion, Asana, ClickUp, monday.com)

Good for documentation, task management, projects. Each area has a space, projects have an owner, tasks have a deadline.

Strengths: durable documentation, progress visualization, customization.

Weaknesses: operational data (sales, finance, HR) still lives somewhere else. The platform becomes yet another separate information layer.

Typical cost: R$50–150 per user/month.

Category 3, Integrated management platform with embedded chat

A single platform that combines BPMS + CRM + finance + indicators + HR with operational chat embedded and connected to real data. A question about a customer is answered with CRM data. A question about an order pulls operational status. A discussion about an indicator happens inside the dashboard.

Strengths: communication connected to data, no information islands, embedded agentic AI, total reduction of tools.

Weaknesses: newer model, fewer options on the market, requires migrating current chat and tools.

Typical cost: R$3–15k/month for the whole company (not per user).

Comparison: which should you choose?

Criterion Chat (Slack) Process (Notion) Integrated platform
Does it solve data fragmentation? No No Yes
Everyday communication Yes Limited Yes
Durable documentation No Yes Yes
Connection to real data No No Yes
Agentic AI connected to operations Limited Limited Yes
Cost (40 employees) R$1.2–4k/month R$2–6k/month R$3–15k/month total
Does it replace other tools? No Partially Yes (several)
Suitable for Any company Project teams B2B 30–300+ employees

How to decide

Use corporate chat (Slack/Teams) if: everyday communication is the main bottleneck and you do not have a data fragmentation problem. It works well as a complement, rarely as a standalone solution.

Use a process platform (Notion/Asana) if: documentation and project management are the main bottleneck. Each area already has its operational tools working.

Use an integrated management platform if: you have data fragmentation across 5+ tools, areas conflict due to lack of a unified view, and you want to reduce the total stack. For a Brazilian B2B company with R$500k+/month, it is usually the better cost-benefit.

Combine two or more when: a mature company uses chat (Slack) for quick conversation + an integrated platform for operations. Each one serves a specific function.

How agentic AI changes the choice in 2026

Modern integrated platforms have an embedded AI agent that changes the equation:

1. Contextual answers with real data. "Status of customer X?" in plain Slack = nobody answers until someone reads it. The same question on an integrated platform = the agent answers with current order, invoice, NPS, and last-contact data.

2. Proactive cross-functional notification. The agent alerts relevant areas when something happens, without anyone needing to remember to communicate.

3. Context translation between areas. A salesperson asks about availability. The agent looks in operations, translates into commercial language, and replies in the channel.

Without agentic AI, a communication platform is just another layer. With agentic AI, it becomes a cross-functional operating system.

Next steps

  1. Identify the real bottleneck. Is it everyday communication? Documentation? Data fragmentation? The answer directs the choice.
  2. List current tools and cost. How many would an integrated platform replace?
  3. Book demos of the 2 main options. Compare in practice.

The worst decision is buying Slack thinking it will solve data fragmentation.

Want to see an integrated platform with operational chat + agentic AI?

A 30-minute demo. Orbit combines operational chat connected to CRM, finance, indicators, and processes, with Olívia responding proactively. Companies with R$500k+/month leave with an applicable diagnosis.

Schedule a demo →

Frequently asked questions

Slack vs Microsoft Teams vs an integrated platform?

Slack and Teams are corporate chat, good for everyday conversation, and they do not solve data fragmentation. An integrated platform combines operational chat with CRM + finance + processes + indicators. For B2B with R$500k+/month, an integrated platform usually has a better cost-benefit.

How much does a corporate communication platform cost?

Slack/Teams: R$30–100/user/month = R$1.2–4k for 40 employees. Notion/Asana: R$50–150/user/month = R$2–6k. Integrated platform: R$3–15k/month for the whole company (not per user). An integrated platform replaces several other tools.

Does an integrated platform replace Slack?

In part. An integrated platform has embedded operational chat, good for conversations connected to real data. Plain Slack has better general chat, good for social/everyday conversation. Mature companies often use both, each serving a specific function.

How does agentic AI change corporate communication?

Three capabilities: contextual answers with real data (not only conversation between humans), proactive cross-functional notification, and context translation between areas. It drastically reduces “nobody told me” as an error category.

When does it make sense to combine Slack + an integrated platform?

Companies that want to keep social/cultural communication in Slack and migrate operational communication to an integrated platform. Each one does what it does best. Total cost is higher, but efficiency goes up.

How do you measure whether a communication platform is working?

Four indicators: reduction of “nobody told me,” reduction of cross-functional coordination time, increase in internal NPS, reduction of “alignment” meetings. A good platform reduces all four in 60–90 days.

Can I solve this without a new platform?

In part. A cross-functional ritual + shared metrics solve 50–60% of the problem. But if data fragmentation across separate systems persists, communication will always fail; the right platform solves it structurally.

How long does implementation take?

Slack/Teams: days. Notion/Asana: weeks. Integrated platform: 1–3 months (because it migrates more than chat). Real team adoption time is longer in all cases; cultural change accompanies technical change.

software-rh-como-escolher.title: HR software for B2B companies: how to choose in 2026
software-rh-como-escolher.excerpt: Separate payroll and HR admin, an HR suite, or an integrated platform? See how to choose HR software for a Brazilian B2B company doing R$500k+/month.
software-rh-como-escolher.content:
To choose HR software for a Brazilian B2B company, distinguish four categories: pure payroll + HR admin software (transactional focus), an HR suite (Convenia, Gupy, Sólides, covering R&S, onboarding, performance), an HR module in a traditional ERP (TOTVS, Sankhya), and an integrated management platform with an HR module (Orbit and similar). Each category serves a different profile, and the wrong choice becomes one more silo separated from the other areas. For a company doing R$500 thousand/month or more with 30–300 employees, an integrated platform often delivers a better cost-benefit ratio because it connects HR to KPIs, processes, and finance.

This article is for managers deciding on new HR software or replacing the current one. It is not a product review; it is a decision framework between architectural categories.

The 4 categories of HR software in the Brazilian market

Category 1, Pure payroll + HR admin (Senior HCM, Microsiga RH, accounting systems)

Transactional focus: payroll, eSocial, FGTS, INSS, vacation, termination. Tax and labor compliance. Generally weak in people-management capabilities (R&S, performance, IDP, retention).

When it makes sense: a company that outsources strategic HR and needs compliance only. Usually complemented by an external accountant.

Cost: R$300–2,000/month for a 40-employee company.

Category 2, HR suite (Convenia, Gupy, Sólides, Pin People)

Covers payroll + the full HR cycle: recruiting and selection, onboarding, performance review, IDP, training, climate surveys, employer branding.

When it makes sense: a company with active strategic HR, a focus on people development, priority on modern capabilities (people analytics, AI in recruiting).

Strengths: advanced HR-specific capabilities, modern interfaces, focus on employee UX.

Weaknesses: integration with finance/CRM/processes depends on API. HR remains a separate silo.

Cost: R$2–15k/month depending on modules and size.

Category 3, HR module in a traditional ERP (TOTVS, SAP, Sankhya)

An HR module as part of a larger ERP. Employee data, payroll, and accounting in the same system.

When it makes sense: an ERP-centric company, large industry, priority on tax/accounting consistency.

Strengths: native integration with finance/accounting, market standard in industry.

Weaknesses: strategic HR capabilities (modern R&S, performance review, people analytics) often weak. Dated UX.

Cost: generally included in the ERP.

Category 4, Integrated management platform with an HR module (Orbit and similar)

An HR module inside a single platform that combines BPMS + CRM + finance + KPIs + HR with an agentic AI agent.

When it makes sense: a B2B company doing R$500k+/month with 30–300 employees, looking to reduce the total number of tools, valuing native integration between areas.

Strengths: HR talks natively with finance (people cost, hiring ROI), KPIs (turnover, eNPS), processes (HR workflows integrated with the rest). Agentic AI detects risk patterns.

Weaknesses: depth in very specific capabilities (advanced R&S with AI) may be lower than a specialized suite.

Cost: R$3–15k/month for the whole company (not per user).

Practical comparison

Criterion Payroll + HR admin HR suite HR in ERP Integrated platform
Labor compliance Strong Medium-strong Strong Medium-strong
Modern R&S Weak Strong Weak-medium Medium-strong
Performance/IDP Weak Strong Medium Medium-strong
People analytics Weak Strong Medium Strong
Integration with finance Manual Via API Native Native
Integration with KPIs/CRM Manual Via API Limited Native
Embedded agentic AI No Some Rare Yes
Cost (40 employees, monthly) R$300-2k R$2-15k Included in ERP R$3-15k total
Suitable for Company that outsources HR Active strategic HR ERP-centric industry B2B 30-300+ employees

How to choose: 5 criteria

1. HR maturity in your company. Transactional HR (payroll only): category 1 is enough. Active strategic HR (R&S, performance, IDP): category 2 or 4. A company that wants to modernize HR: category 4 with AI.

2. Importance of integration with other areas. If HR decisions need to talk with finance, CRM, processes: category 3 or 4. If HR can be a separate silo: category 2 works.

3. Total cost of ownership. Add license + integrations + maintenance. For a mid-sized B2B company, category 4 often wins on TCO because it eliminates other tools.

4. Specific capabilities needed. A company that needs a very advanced R&S capability with AI: category 2 (Gupy). A company that needs people analytics integrated with business KPIs: category 4.

5. Implementation speed. Integrated platform: 1–3 months. HR suite: 1–2 months per module. ERP: 6–18 months.

Decision tree

Question 1: Does the company fully outsource strategic HR?

  • Yes: category 1 (payroll + HR admin). Go to implementation.
  • No: continue.

Question 2: Is the company a large industrial with a strong ERP?

  • Yes: HR module in the current ERP. Go to implementation.
  • No: continue.

Question 3: Does HR need very specific capabilities (advanced R&S, complex performance)?

  • Yes: category 2 (specialized HR suite) + integration with other areas via API.
  • No: continue.

Question 4: Is the company looking to reduce the total number of tools and have an integrated view?

  • Yes: category 4 (integrated platform). Generally the better cost-benefit for Brazilian B2B doing R$500k+/month.
  • No: combine category 1 + 2.

How agentic AI changes HR software in 2026

Three capabilities:

1. Real-time attrition-risk detection. The agent crosses KPIs (engagement, performance, feedback frequency) and flags talent at risk 60–90 days before they resign.

2. Candidate suggestion based on cultural fit. In recruiting, the agent analyzes the candidate profile + the profile of people who succeeded at the company and proposes an adjustment to the selection process.

3. Personalized IDP per employee. For each person, it suggests a development path, courses, mentoring, aligned with aspirations and the company's needs.

In Orbit, Olívia operates these three capabilities integrated with the HR module + KPIs.

Next steps

  1. Identify your stage. Transactional HR, active strategic, or modernizing? The answer points to the category.
  2. Calculate the total cost of current HR tools (payroll, ATS, performance review, eNPS). Compare with an integrated platform.
  3. Book a demo of the 2 best options. Compare in practice, not on a slide.

The worst decision is to stay with HR software that clearly does not meet your needs, waiting to "mature more before deciding".

Want to see an HR module integrated with finance, KPIs, and AI?

A 30-minute demo. Orbit combines an HR module with CRM, finance, and KPIs, with Olívia detecting attrition risk and suggesting a personalized IDP. Companies doing R$500k+/month leave with an applicable diagnosis.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best HR software for a B2B company?

It depends on the stage. Transactional HR: payroll + HR admin is enough. Active strategic HR: an HR suite (Convenia, Gupy) or an integrated platform. A B2B company doing R$500k+/month with 30–300 employees: an integrated platform usually has a better cost-benefit ratio.

How much does HR software cost?

Pure payroll + HR admin: R$300–2k/month. HR suite: R$2–15k/month depending on modules. ERP with an HR module: included. Integrated platform: R$3–15k/month for the whole company (not per user, includes other areas).

Are Convenia, Gupy, and Sólides the same?

They are all Brazilian HR suites with different specific strengths. Convenia: payroll + HR admin + onboarding. Gupy: strong in R&S with AI. Sólides: strong in assessment and culture. Each has a different focus; evaluate which capability is most critical for your company.

Can I have HR software without changing ERP?

Yes. Specialized HR software + the current ERP can coexist via API integration. The limit: two systems to keep updated. An integrated platform removes that limit by having everything natively connected.

How long does implementation take?

Payroll + HR admin: 2–4 weeks. HR suite: 1–2 months per module. HR in ERP: included in ERP implementation. Integrated platform: 1–3 months. Real team adoption time is always longer; plan for cultural change.

How does AI change HR software in 2026?

Three capabilities: real-time attrition-risk detection, candidate suggestion with cultural fit, personalized IDP per employee. Agentic AI turns HR from transactional to predictive.

Does an integrated platform replace Convenia/Gupy?

In part. It covers labor compliance, performance review, IDP, people analytics. It may be less deep in very specific capabilities (advanced high-volume R&S, complex psychometric assessment). For a mid-sized B2B company, it replaces well; for a company with intense recruiting, it may complement.

How do you measure ROI of HR software?

Turnover reduction (cost avoided per departure), time-to-hire (financial impact of an open role), team productivity (administrative capacity freed up), employee satisfaction (eNPS). Good software changes all 4 KPIs in 6–12 months.

como-automatizar-processos-empresa.title: How to automate company processes: the definitive guide for companies doing R$500k+/month
como-automatizar-processos-empresa.excerpt: Already mapped and ready to automate? See the 4 paths (DIY, no-code, BPMS, custom), the ROI math, and the 10 processes every B2B company should automate first.
como-automatizar-processos-empresa.content:
To automate company processes, you first identify repetitive processes with clear rules, choose one of the four available automation paths (DIY integrators, no-code platform, integrated BPMS, or custom development), implement in order of impact, and measure ROI month by month. In Brazilian B2B companies at R$500 thousand/month or more with 30 to 300 employees, the most frequent path in 2026 is BPMS integrated with AI agents, because it eliminates tool fragmentation, generates return in 90 days, and grows with the operation.

This article is the third in a series on processes. If you haven’t yet mapped the critical processes of your business, start with How to organize processes in a company that grew fast — automating without mapping is putting gasoline into an operation that still has no direction. If you’re only now recognizing that manual processes are stalling growth, read first Why manual processes are stalling your company’s growth.

From here on, we assume you’ve already understood the problem and mapped the critical processes. Now the game is an implementation decision.

Before automating: the 3 questions that filter what should (and shouldn’t) be automated

Not every process should be automated. Trying to automate everything is the second most expensive mistake in automation projects (behind only trying to automate without mapping). Before touching any process, answer three questions:

1. Is the process repetitive enough? Automation only pays off when the process runs at least a few times per week. A process that happens once a quarter rarely justifies the automation investment — it’s better to have a clear SOP and let a human execute it.

2. Are the execution rules clear (without subjective judgment)? Automation works with logic. If the process requires "it depends on the case", "it varies by client", or "the way Maria does it", automating will create more problems than it solves. Before automating, standardize the rules.

3. Does the volume justify the investment? Calculate: time spent per execution × frequency × cost of the executor’s hour = current annual cost. Compare with the cost of automation (tool + implementation). If the current cost doesn’t cover 12 months of automation, wait or prioritize another process.

The practical rule: automate first the processes that combine high frequency (several times per week or day), clear rules (binary logical decision), and high volume (a lot of human time consumed). Those are where ROI appears fastest.

The 10 processes every B2B company should automate first

In more than 3,000 implementations in mid-sized Brazilian companies, ten processes appear repeatedly as the highest-ROI ones when automated. Start with these:

1. New client registration and onboarding. When the contract closes, automatically: creates a CRM record, sends a welcome email, notifies the CX team, schedules the kickoff, generates the first invoice. What used to take 2h becomes 2 minutes of review.

2. Generation and sending of commercial proposals. Pre-formatted template, filled with CRM data, generated as PDF and sent to the prospect with a digital signature link. A salesperson who spent 45min per proposal now spends 5min.

3. Discount or commercial exception approval. Rule: up to X% discount, the salesperson approves alone. Above X%, it automatically triggers approval to the manager with a 4h deadline. Above Y%, it escalates to the director. Ends loose WhatsApp and email.

4. Boleto matching and settlement. Integration between bank and finance: boleto paid → status updated in the system → CRM marked → confirmation email to the client → receipt generated. Eliminates 1-2h daily from finance.

5. Issuing and sending the tax invoice. Triggered when the order is billed, with no need to copy data from system to system. Reduces tax error and close time.

6. Nurture / lifecycle email dispatch. A new client receives a sequence of 5 onboarding emails in the first 3 weeks. A client idle for 60 days receives reactivation. Contract anniversary pulls an NPS survey. Basic marketing automation.

7. Order status updates for the client. The client receives an automatic notification when the order leaves the factory, when it ships, when it arrives. Reduces “where’s my order?” tickets by 60-80%.

8. Generation of weekly and monthly reports. Dashboards updated in real time, with automatic send every Monday morning to the leadership team. Ends the entire Friday someone loses closing a spreadsheet.

9. Contract renewal reminder. 90 days before expiration, it triggers a task for the account manager. 60 days before, an email to the client. 30 days before, escalation to the manager. Recovers revenue that is often lost to forgetfulness.

10. NPS and satisfaction feedback collection. 30 days after onboarding, automatic email with NPS. A score below 7 triggers an alert to the CX team. A score above 9 becomes an automatic referral request.

Don’t try to automate all 10 at once. Start with 2-3 and stabilize before moving forward.

The 4 automation paths: how to choose the right one

There are four paths to automate processes, and the wrong choice is expensive. Each one has a clear trade-off:

Path 1, DIY integrators (Zapier, Make, n8n)

What it is: low-code tools that connect existing applications via pre-built integrations. You define "when this happens in X, do Y in Z".

When to use it: point automations between 2-3 systems, simple and well-defined processes, a team without dedicated IT.

Advantages: low cost (USD 20-100/month), implementation in hours, thousands of ready connectors.

Limits: complexity explodes quickly. Above 10 interconnected automations, it becomes “spaghetti” that’s hard to maintain. Doesn’t support processes with complex conditional logic. No unified view of what’s running.

Typical cost: R$200-2,000/month for a 40-person company. Recommended for: initial validation, edge automations, a complement to other solutions.

Path 2, No-code workflow platform (Pipefy, monday.com, Process.st)

What it is: a platform dedicated to designing and running workflows, with a visual “drag and drop” interface. Each process becomes a pipe/board.

When to use it: operations or process teams want autonomy to create and modify workflows without IT; processes with multiple sequential steps; approvals and forms.

Advantages: friendly interface, fast process creation, good for linear flows and approvals.

Limits: each process is an island. When you need the sales process to talk to the finance process, it becomes a manual API integration. Operations indicators stay separate from business numbers. Cost grows quickly per user.

Typical cost: R$1,500-8,000/month for a 40-person company. Recommended for: teams that want operational autonomy without IT, support processes (compliance, purchasing, human resources).

Path 3, BPMS integrated with AI (Orbit, TOTVS Fluig, SAP)

What it is: a platform that combines process management (BPMS) with integrated CRM, finance, indicators, HR, and internal communication modules, often with an embedded AI agent.

When to use it: a company at R$500 thousand/month or more, 30 to 300 employees, with a need for processes talking to finance and indicators; wants to reduce the total number of tools; seeks growth without doubling headcount.

Advantages: one platform only, processes connected to business data, an AI agent that learns from real operations, scales with the company without a stack migration.

Limits: a larger investment than paths 1 and 2. Requires leadership alignment around operating on a single platform.

Typical cost: R$3,000-15,000/month for a 40-person company (varies a lot by vendor). Recommended for: mid-sized Brazilian B2B companies that want to consolidate the stack and scale without losing control.

Orbit operates in this category — 20 integrated modules, Olívia (AI agent) that maps processes by conversational interview and monitors execution in real time, and a focus on B2B ICP of R$500k+/month.

Path 4, Custom development

What it is: your own technology team (or a consulting firm) develops the automation from scratch, custom-built.

When to use it: a unique process, with a real competitive advantage, that no platform covers; companies with mature IT and the capacity to maintain their own code.

Advantages: full control, fine-tuning possible, vendor independence.

Limits: the most expensive, the slowest, and the riskiest. Ongoing maintenance is expensive. In 90% of cases, a path 3 platform covers 95% of needs at a fraction of the cost.

Typical cost: R$50,000-500,000 per project + R$20,000-80,000/year of maintenance. Recommended for: only processes that are a unique competitive advantage and that don’t exist in the category.

Quick comparison

Criterion Path 1 (DIY) Path 2 (No-code) Path 3 (BPMS+AI) Path 4 (Custom)
Initial cost Very low Medium Medium-high Very high
Implementation time Hours Weeks 1-3 months 6-18 months
Scalability Low Medium High High
Maintenance Manual Internal team Vendor Internal team
Integrated view No No Yes Depends
Indicated company size <30 employees 30-100 30-300+ 100+ with mature IT

How much it costs to automate (and how much it costs not to automate)

The question isn’t "how much does it cost to automate?" — it’s "how much does it cost NOT to automate?". For a typical Brazilian B2B company with 40 employees and R$1 million in monthly revenue, the realistic calculation is as follows:

Current annual cost of the manual operation:

  • Silent rework (estimated at 61% of rework tied to manuals, according to CIO/Camunda 2020 research): R$1.2-1.4 million/year
  • Unnecessary hires from lack of process (4 people/year on average): R$384 thousand/year
  • Above-market client churn (dissatisfaction from inconsistency): R$200-400 thousand/year
  • Estimated total: R$1.8-2.2 million/year

Typical automation investment (path 3, integrated BPMS):

  • Platform: R$60-180 thousand/year
  • Initial implementation: R$30-80 thousand (one-time)
  • Internal training: R$10-20 thousand
  • Year 1 total: R$100-280 thousand. From year 2: R$60-180 thousand

Typical payback: 4-7 months. Year 1 ROI: 6-10x. Year 3 ROI (cumulative): 25-40x.

These numbers are conservative and vary by sector. But the fundamental relationship holds: the cost of delaying automation is always greater than the cost of implementing it, in any company that has crossed the 30-employee barrier.

The role of AI in modern automation (and why 2026 changes the game)

Classic automation (pre-2024) worked on top of rules: "if X happens, do Y". All logic had to be designed in advance. Every exception had to be anticipated. When the process changed, the automation stopped working until someone updated the rule.

Modern automation, with AI agents, does three things classic automation didn’t:

1. Mapping by conversational interview. Instead of you sitting down and drawing a flowchart, the agent interviews the team: "what happens when a new client closes a contract?". From the answers, it builds the structured mapping, identifies gaps, proposes improvements. What used to take 3 days of a consultant takes 3 hours.

2. Automatic generation of workflows + documentation. From the mapping, the agent creates the executable workflow, the written SOP, the visual flowchart, and the checklist in parallel. You review and adjust — you don’t write from scratch.

3. Contextual monitoring with improvement suggestions. The agent observes execution in real time and identifies bottlenecks with context: "the proposal approval process averages 4 days, but 80% of the delay is concentrated in legal review. Suggestions: create an automatic track for contracts below R$50k, or hire a part-time reviewer. Impact estimate: reduce SLA to 1.5 days."

It isn’t an assistant that answers a question — it’s an agent that operates alongside the team, learns from the company’s real operations, and suggests changes based on data, not a generic manual.

At Orbit, that role is played by Olívia, an AI agent integrated with the platform’s 20 modules. It isn’t a chatbot; it’s an operational layer that connects processes, indicators, finance, and CRM, and acts proactively on them.

Why this matters in 2026: companies that keep automating "the 2022 way" will scale linearly. Companies that adopt automation with agentic AI scale exponentially, because the time between "deciding to change a process" and "having the new process running" dropped from months to hours.

The 7 steps to implement automation in 90 days

A condensed playbook, tested in Brazilian companies from R$500k to R$5M/month.

Weeks 1-2: Diagnosis and prioritization

List the company processes that run at least 5 times per week. For each one: average execution time, number of people involved, error frequency, key-person dependency. Prioritize 3 processes with the highest product (time × frequency × cost). Those are the first candidates.

Weeks 3-4: Real mapping (not ideal)

For each of the 3 priority processes, observe real execution — not what’s documented, not what it should be. Use screen video if needed. List each step, decision, system used, communication exchanged. Result: 3 process maps in hand.

Week 5: Path choice

With the maps in hand, decide: path 1, 2, 3, or 4. Use the comparison table above. For a company with 30-300 employees that needs an integrated view, the answer is most often path 3 (BPMS + AI).

Weeks 6-9: Pilot process implementation

Implement ONE of the 3 processes as a pilot. Not all three. Configure the tool, train 1-2 people, run it with the real team, adjust. By the end of week 9, the pilot process should be running stably.

Weeks 10-11: Implementation of the other 2

Replicate the pilot method for the other 2 processes. Faster because now you already know.

Weeks 12-13: Measurement and adjustment

Measure “before” and “after” for the 3 processes: average time, error rate, human dependency, team satisfaction. Report to leadership. Decide the next 3 processes to automate.

In 90 days, with this playbook, it is realistic to expect: 3 critical processes automated, a 30-50% reduction in total time dedicated to them, and absolute clarity on what the next steps are.

The 5 mistakes that stall automation projects

Patterns observed in projects that didn’t take off:

1. Wanting to automate everything at once. The company announces "we’re going to digitize everything in 6 months" and spends 6 months delivering nothing. Start small, prove, expand.

2. Choosing the tool before mapping the process. The tool should serve the process, not the other way around. Teams that buy a platform without mapping end up molding the process to the tool, and ROI disappears.

3. Not involving the people who execute. Automation imposed by the owner or IT without consulting the people who do the work today generates active resistance. The person who executes today knows details nobody else knows — and if ignored, they break the automation.

4. Forgetting to measure the before. Without a baseline (average time before automation, error rate before), you can never prove ROI. Worse: you never learn what works.

5. Treating automation as a project, not as a continuous practice. A well-automated process today becomes obsolete in 12-18 months if nobody reviews it. Automation is a continuous improvement practice, not a one-off event.

Practical next steps

If you made it this far, three actions for this week:

  1. List the 5 processes that run most in your company per week. Execution time × frequency × hourly cost = return potential.
  2. For the 3 with the highest potential, choose which automation path makes sense. Use the table above as a guide.
  3. Book a demonstration of the options that fit your case — don’t decide without seeing the tool working in your scenario.

The worst decision is not deciding. The second worst is deciding without comparing.

Want to see how Orbit’s BPMS + AI works in your scenario?

In a 30-minute demonstration, we show how Orbit automates your company’s processes with 20 integrated modules (Processes, CRM, Finance, Indicators, HR, and more) operated by Olívia, an AI agent that learns from your business’s real operations. Companies at R$500 thousand/month or more leave the meeting with an applicable diagnosis, an example of the first 3 processes to automate, and an ROI estimate.

Schedule a demonstration →

Frequently asked questions about process automation

How do you start automating processes in the company?

Start by listing the processes that run at least 5 times per week. For the 3 with the highest product of time × frequency × cost, observe real execution (not the ideal). Choose an automation path (DIY, no-code, BPMS+AI, or custom) based on size and need. Implement ONE process as a pilot before scaling to the other 2.

Which tools should you use to automate processes?

It depends on the path. For point automations between systems: Zapier, Make, or n8n. For workflows with approval and forms: Pipefy or monday.com. For B2B companies at R$500 thousand/month or more that need processes talking to CRM, finance, and indicators in a single platform: BPMS integrated with AI, the category Orbit belongs to.

How much does it cost to automate processes in a company?

For a B2B company with 40 people, typical costs by path are: DIY integrators from R$200 to R$2,000/month; no-code platform from R$1,500 to R$8,000/month; integrated BPMS from R$3,000 to R$15,000/month; custom development from R$50,000 to R$500,000 per project. Typical payback on any path is between 4 and 7 months.

What’s the difference between automation and process automatization?

Automation refers to processes that run fully without human intervention (RPA, IoT sensors, industrial robots). Automatization is the use of technology to accelerate processes while keeping human intervention at decision or supervision points. In day-to-day B2B practice, the terms are often used as synonyms.

What can be automated in a company?

The 10 processes most commonly automated in Brazilian B2B companies: client registration/onboarding, proposal generation, discount approval, boleto matching, invoice issuance, nurture email, order status updates, weekly report generation, contract renewal reminder, and NPS collection. These 10 cover ~70% of typical mid-market automation return.

How long does it take to automate all processes?

The 3 critical processes can be automated in 60-90 days following a structured playbook. Mapping and automating the entire operation takes between 9 and 18 months, depending on size and the path chosen. But most of the ROI appears in the first 90 days with the 3 critical processes — the rest is incremental optimization.

Can I automate processes without dedicated IT?

Yes, especially on paths 1 (DIY with Zapier/Make) and 3 (no-code BPMS with AI). Modern platforms are designed so operations people can configure flows without code. For path 4 (custom development), dedicated IT is mandatory. For the other three paths, someone on the team with an “operations + basic technology” profile is usually enough.

How do you measure process automation ROI?

Before automating, capture a baseline: average execution time, number of people involved, error rate, rework frequency. After automation, capture the same numbers. ROI is: (monthly cost avoided × 12) ÷ (automation cost in year 1). In typical mid-sized Brazilian B2B cases, year 1 ROI is between 6x and 10x.

dre-tempo-real.title: Real-time P&L: the complete guide to financial visibility in 2026
dre-tempo-real.excerpt: A P&L closed on the 10th of the following month is obsolete. See how to implement a real-time P&L, a comparison of 4 paths, and what changed in 2026 with AI.
dre-tempo-real.content:
A real-time DRE is the version of the income statement (Demonstração de Resultado do Exercício) updated continuously as company transactions happen, instead of monthly after the accounting close. It lets the manager see the likely result for the month on any given day, decide during the month (not after it), and identify margin deviations before they become a crisis. In 2026, at Brazilian B2B companies of R$500,000/month or more, a real-time DRE is no longer an advanced feature — it has become a basic requirement of competitive financial management.

This article is for anyone who already understands that month-end finance is not enough and is deciding which architecture to use to implement a real-time DRE. If you have not yet named the problem, it is worth reading first Why your company sells a lot and still runs short of cash or Integrated financial management: how to get a real view of the business.

From here on, we cover: what a real-time DRE is and what it is not, the 6 elements every implementation needs, a comparison of the 4 available paths, the decision criteria for choosing yours, and how agentic AI changes the game from 2026 on.

What a real-time DRE is (and what it is NOT)

A real-time DRE is an operational layer of financial management that shows, in real time or close to it, the likely state of the month's result — recognized revenue, posted costs, allocated expenses, calculated margin. It works like a cockpit instrument: the pilot does not wait until landing to know they are off course.

What it is:

  • Updated as events occur (deal closed, invoice issued, expense posted, cost applied)
  • Fed automatically by operational systems (CRM, finance, accounting, HR)
  • Available as a navigable dashboard + an exportable report
  • Comparable with target, prior month, and the same period last year
  • Granular by business line, product, segment, and cost center

What it is NOT:

  • A substitute for the official accounting close (that remains monthly, formal, and validated by the accountant)
  • Just a pretty revenue dashboard (a DRE needs to cover revenue, cost, expense, and result)
  • Something you build only with BI on top of a spreadsheet (BI on bad data is still bad data)
  • A feature only for large companies (in 2026, it is viable at any B2B company of R$500k+/month)

The most common confusion is thinking that "having a revenue dashboard" is the same as "having a real-time DRE." It is not. A revenue dashboard shows inflow. A DRE shows the result — revenue minus cost minus expense.

The 6 elements every real-time DRE implementation needs

The pattern observed in companies that implemented it and kept it working for 12+ months:

1. Automatic capture of recognized revenue. When a salesperson closes a deal in the CRM, the event automatically triggers a recognized-revenue record with the correct date. Without automatic capture, someone has to post it manually, and delay or error kills the real-time quality.

2. Unit cost updated by product/service line. Each product/service needs a registered and updated unit cost. When raw materials go up, when freight gets more expensive, when the acquirer fee gets worse, the cost recalculates automatically.

3. Fixed expense allocated proportionally to the current month. Payroll, rent, corporate software, accounting, monthly expenses. In real time, they are allocated by business day, so on day 15 of the month the DRE already reflects 50% of expected fixed expense.

4. Correct accounting recognition (accrual principle). Cash came in but the service was not delivered? It is not revenue yet. The service was delivered but cash has not come in? It is revenue. A real-time DRE needs to respect accrual accounting, not confuse it with cash flow.

5. Automatic comparison (vs target, MoM, YoY). A number on its own says nothing. R$420k of recognized revenue on day 15 — is that good or bad? It depends on the R$1M target, on the same period last month, on last year. A good dashboard shows all three comparisons.

6. Drill-down to the data source. Margin dropped 5%? Click the number and see: which product, which customer, which specific sale is pulling the average down. Without drill-down, a real-time DRE is just a pretty report, not a decision tool.

Missing any one of these 6 elements does not invalidate the DRE, but it reduces practical usefulness. Missing 3 or more means you have a dashboard, not a real-time DRE.

The 4 paths to implement a real-time DRE (compared)

Path 1: Automated spreadsheet + scheduled import

What it is: a spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel + macro) that automatically imports data from other systems via API, updates formulas, and generates a consolidated view.

When it makes sense: a company with up to 15 employees, data in a few systems, simple processes, no dedicated IT but someone with average technical knowledge.

Advantages: almost zero cost, full control over the format.

Limits: it breaks easily; configuration work remains manual; it does not support sophisticated drill-down; high risk of formula error; it does not support sustained growth.

Cost: R$0–200/month. The truth: it almost always becomes "DRE the next day," not real time.

Path 2: ERP with an automated DRE module

What it is: a traditional ERP (TOTVS, Sankhya, SAP, Senior) with a robust finance module and a DRE report generated automatically from system entries.

When it makes sense: an ERP-centric company, with most transactions already entering through the ERP.

Advantages: consistent accounting data; native integration with the official close; a market standard.

Limits: updates are generally not instant (D+1 or D+2 is typical); limited customization; areas outside the ERP (marketing, support) are left out.

Cost: usually included in the ERP license. The truth: "real time" is often D+1 in disguise.

Path 3: BI platform + system integration (Power BI, Looker, Tableau)

What it is: pure BI that consumes data from multiple systems (ERP, CRM, bank), unifies it in a data warehouse, and generates custom DRE dashboards.

When it makes sense: a company with dedicated IT and a data analyst; a need to cross different sources; a desire for advanced visualization customization.

Advantages: very high analytical power; full flexibility; sophisticated visualization.

Limits: requires a trained BI analyst; high total cost (tool + analyst); dependent on whoever builds/maintains the dashboard; keeps the data in separate systems.

Cost: R$10–23k/month (license + BI analyst). The truth: powerful, but it requires a dedicated team.

Path 4: Integrated management platform with a native real-time DRE

What it is: a unified platform (BPMS + CRM + finance + indicators) where the DRE is a native module, fed in real time by events from the other modules.

When it makes sense: a Brazilian B2B company at R$500k+/month, 30–300 employees, looking to reduce the total number of tools, wanting a truly real-time DRE (not D+1), and valuing operational simplicity.

Advantages: a truly real-time DRE (not D+1); native integration with sales, finance, and processes; an AI agent monitors deviations automatically; competitive total cost.

Limits: a higher initial investment than a spreadsheet; it may require migrating data from legacy tools.

Cost: R$3–15k/month depending on size. The truth: the path with the best cost-benefit for the ICP described.

The Orbit operates in this category, with 20 integrated modules and Olívia, an agent that monitors the DRE continuously.

Quick comparison

Criterion Spreadsheet ERP Pure BI Integrated platform
Truly real time? No Typical D+1 Possible Yes
Requires IT/analyst? No No Yes No
Native drill-down? Limited Yes Yes Yes
Does AI monitor deviations? No No Some Yes
Monthly cost R$0–200 Included in ERP R$10–23k R$3–15k
Implementation time Immediate Included 3–6 months 1–3 months
Suitable for <15 employees ERP-centric company Dedicated IT 30–300+ employees

How to choose the path: 5 decision criteria

1. Is true real time critical? For some companies, D+1 is already enough. For others (retail, e-commerce, high pricing volatility), it needs to be live. If you make intra-day or intra-week decisions, you need true real time.

2. Internal technical capacity. Pure BI requires an analyst. An integrated platform and an ERP work without dedicated IT. Assess what you have available.

3. Transaction volume. A company with 30 sales/month can operate well with a spreadsheet. A company with 3,000 sales/month cannot — human error accumulates.

4. Total cost of ownership over 3 years. Consider license + implementation + maintenance + analyst + downtime. At an average Brazilian B2B company, an integrated platform usually wins.

5. Process maturity. Without a digitized process, financial data stays manual and a real-time DRE is theory. Before buying a tool, make sure sales, billing, and accounts payable/receivable live in a system (not in a parallel spreadsheet).

How agentic AI changes the real-time DRE in 2026

Until 2024, a real-time DRE was a passive tool: the manager opened it, looked, interpreted, acted. With agentic AI, the flow reverses — the agent monitors the DRE 24/7 and only talks to you when something requires action. Three practical cases:

1. Detecting margin erosion before the close. "Gross margin on product X dropped 6% over the last 3 weeks. Likely cause: cost increase in raw material Y (traced in 4 supplier invoices). Suggestion: review pricing or negotiate with the supplier. Estimated impact if you do not act: -R$32k on the quarter's result."

2. Alert on negative margin in a specific sale. "3 deals closed this week have real margin below 5%, below company policy. Salesperson: João. Customer: Acme. I recommend reviewing the approved discounts."

3. Dynamic projection of the monthly result. "Based on the pattern of the last 6 months and transactions in the first 15 days, the likely result for the month is R$340k (vs a R$400k target). The 3 factors with the largest negative impact: a sales drop in segment X, a cost increase in product Y, a delayed receipt from customer Z."

That level of proactivity changes the CFO's role: from someone who reports the past to someone who guides the future in advance.

At Orbit, Olívia does exactly that, connected to the finance + CRM + indicators + processes modules.

Practical next steps

If you decided you need a real-time DRE, three actions:

  1. Map every point where financial data enters today. How many systems, how many manual entries, what is the typical delay until consolidation.
  2. Identify which of the 4 paths makes sense for your company. Use the 5 decision criteria above.
  3. Book a demo of the 2 main options. Do not decide without seeing the tool operating in your scenario, with your data.

The worst decision is to keep closing the DRE on the 10th of the following month while competitors decide with yesterday's data.

Frequently asked questions about real-time DRE

What is a real-time DRE?

A version of the income statement updated continuously as company transactions happen, instead of monthly after the close. It lets you see the likely result for the month on any given day and decide during the month.

Does a real-time DRE replace the monthly accounting DRE?

No. The monthly accounting DRE still exists for tax, official, and audit purposes. A real-time DRE is an operational management tool. The two coexist: the operational one informs daily decisions, the official one validates and formalizes.

Which tools generate a real-time DRE?

Four paths: automated spreadsheet (up to 15 employees), ERP with a DRE module (typical D+1), pure BI such as Power BI/Tableau (with dedicated IT), integrated platform with a native real-time DRE (B2B, 30–300 employees). Each serves a profile.

How much does it cost to implement a real-time DRE?

Spreadsheet: R$0–200/month. ERP: usually included. Pure BI: R$10–23k/month (with an analyst). Integrated platform: R$3–15k/month. ROI typically in 4–7 months considering recovered margin and freed-up analytical capacity.

What elements does every real-time DRE need?

Six: automatic revenue capture, updated unit cost, fixed expense allocated by business day, correct accounting recognition (accrual), automatic comparison (vs target, MoM, YoY), drill-down to the source. Missing 3+ means a dashboard, not a real-time DRE.

Can I have a real-time DRE with Excel?

Technically yes, but with limits. Excel works for companies of up to 15 employees, with few integrated systems. Above that, it becomes "DRE the next day," and when it becomes manual, it becomes "DRE at month-end." For true real time in a growing company, a dedicated platform is needed.

How does AI change the DRE in 2026?

Until 2024, the DRE was a passive tool (the manager looks and interprets). With agentic AI, the agent monitors the DRE 24/7 and only speaks when something requires action: detecting margin erosion before the close, alerting on negative margin in specific sales, dynamically projecting the monthly result.

How long does it take to implement a real-time DRE?

Spreadsheet: immediate (days). ERP: included, it usually already exists. Pure BI: 3–6 months (depends on the data warehouse). Integrated platform: 1–3 months. Most of the implementation time is data configuration, not technology.
